articles.title: An Award-Winning Indian Kitchen Is Opening in a Phoenix Mall. That's a Bigger Deal Than It Sounds.
articles.excerpt: NADU, a James Beard semifinalist and Michelin Bib Gourmand winner from Chicago, debuts at Desert Ridge — the latest sign that Indian food in America has stopped apologizing.
articles.image_caption: Tandoori chicken plated with herb rice in a modern fine-dining presentation, reflecting a new wave of regional Indian cooking in America.
articles.nri_angle: For a generation of Indian-Americans who grew up faintly embarrassed by the strip-mall curry house, the rise of regional Indian fine dining is a marker of cultural arrival — food that no longer asks permission to exist in America.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After Three Temples Were Hit in Two Weeks, Hindu Americans Are Done Quietly Repainting the Walls
articles.excerpt: The Hindu American Foundation has formally asked California's hate commission to count anti-Hindu bias — a sign of a diaspora that has decided to be counted.
articles.image_caption: The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Robbinsville, New Jersey, at sunset — one of the landmark Hindu temples built by the American diaspora.
articles.nri_angle: A community that long preferred private success to public advocacy is now writing letters to the state, lodging diplomatic complaints, and installing security cameras — formally demanding recognition among the communities at risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Oldest Indian Association Swore In a New Board. The Guest List Was a Map of How Far the Community Has Come.
articles.excerpt: Founded in 1967 to get Indians counted on the U.S. census, the AIA now draws letters from senators and ambassadors — and faces a generational handover.
articles.image_caption: A community honoree holds an award before an applauding audience, a scene familiar at Indian-American organizational galas.
articles.nri_angle: The endless circuit of diaspora galas serves a real function: it is the connective tissue binding the founders who fought for census recognition to a second generation that no longer needs the organization for survival.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Doctor Born to Immigrants Is About to Spend Eight Months in Orbit. The Diaspora Has a New Kind of Hero.
articles.excerpt: Anil Menon, son of an Indian father and a Ukrainian mother, launches next month on his first spaceflight — a quiet rebuke to anyone who thinks the immigrant story has only one script.
articles.image_caption: NASA astronaut Anil Menon in his official portrait at the Johnson Space Center
articles.nri_angle: Menon's path — Harvard, Stanford, the ER, SpaceX, now the ISS — is the diaspora's familiar overachiever arc bent toward an unfamiliar destination. He represents a generation of Indian-American children no longer choosing between medicine and a dream.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: He Wore No. 10 for New Zealand and Made History for India Without Ever Playing for It
articles.excerpt: Sarpreet Singh became the first player of Indian heritage to start a World Cup match. He is one of at least four at this tournament — a scattered, accidental Indian team playing under other flags.
articles.image_caption: Sarpreet Singh training with FC Bayern Munich in 2019
articles.nri_angle: India has never qualified for a men's World Cup, yet its bloodlines are all over the 2026 tournament — in New Zealand, Australian, Qatari and Congolese shirts. It is the diaspora's strange consolation: present everywhere, representing no one back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Dangled a 7% Dollar Return at the Diaspora. Now Its Banks Are Scrambling to Fund the Promise.
articles.excerpt: The RBI's special deposit window could pull in $55-70 billion from NRIs by September. But behind the headline rates, banks are quietly fighting over who is allowed to make the loans that make the math work.
articles.image_caption: An aerial view of GIFT City, India's tax-neutral financial hub in Gandhinagar, Gujarat
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs, the pitch is simple — a tax-free 7% dollar return from a home-country bank. But the scramble behind the scenes shows how badly India needs the diaspora's savings right now, and how the fine print decides who actually benefits.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Half of America's Motels Have an Indian Owner. San Francisco Is Building Them a Museum.
articles.excerpt: The Tenderloin Museum's permanent Indo-American Hotelier exhibit fixes a diaspora folk fact into history — names, ledgers and all — before the founding generation fades.
articles.image_caption: A classic American roadside motel — the kind of property Gujarati immigrant families built into a nationwide hospitality network (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The Patel-motel story is one of the diaspora's most successful but least celebrated immigrant business sagas — a museum claims it as heritage worth preserving rather than a punchline.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Twenty-Six Years and $8.5 Million Later, a Pennsylvania Temple Opens a School to Outrun Forgetting
articles.excerpt: The Bharatiya Learning Center in Chalfont is the diaspora's bet that cultural continuity needs walls, classrooms and a budget — not just good intentions.
articles.image_caption: A Hindu temple in the United States, where heritage-language education is taking root in the diaspora (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Every immigrant family negotiates the same bargain: let the kids win in America without becoming strangers to their grandparents. This $8.5M center is that bargain built in brick.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A 33-Year-Old Indian Newspaper Just Won Australia's Top Multicultural Prize. The Timing Wasn't an Accident.
articles.excerpt: Indian Link's fifth Best Multicultural Publication win lands in a year of inflated migration claims and anti-immigration marches — an official counter-signal to louder voices.
articles.image_caption: Community-language print media remains one of a diaspora's most durable records of itself (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: When mainstream media covers a diaspora only in moments of conflict, the community's own storytellers become its memory — and its defense. This award honors 33 years of that work.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An H-1B Worker Says He Paid $100,000 to Keep His Job. His Lawsuit Exposes the Visa's Dark Side.
articles.excerpt: A Telugu contract worker's labor-trafficking suit in Michigan alleges 'pay-to-stay' exploitation, withheld pay stubs and threats of ICE — a painful mirror for a diaspora that celebrates its own success.
articles.image_caption: A federal building and US courthouse; an Indian H-1B worker's labor-trafficking suit is moving through the courts
articles.nri_angle: Because the H-1B visa is tied to one employer and Indians face decades-long green-card backlogs, the sponsor holds outsized power — and this lawsuit shows how that power can curdle into forced labor, a warning to the hundreds of thousands of Indians whose American future hangs on a single signature.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The US Embassy Just Told Indian Visa Holders: The Vetting Never Stops — Even After You're Approved
articles.excerpt: A new advisory warns that screening continues after a visa is granted and that 'all available information' stays in play — deepening unease for a community already facing backlogs and 221(g) holds.
articles.image_caption: The US Embassy in New Delhi, which has warned that visa screening continues even after a visa is granted
articles.nri_angle: For the hundreds of thousands of Indians who enter the US each year on student, work and visitor visas, the embassy's warning reframes an approved visa as a continuously reviewed privilege — raising the stakes on social-media posts, travel and everyday life.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 40% of Indian Americans Have Thought About Leaving the US. The 'Reverse Brain Drain' Just Got Its Numbers.
articles.excerpt: A Carnegie Endowment survey of 1,000 Indian Americans finds a community in 'turbulence' — with frustration over politics, cost of living and safety driving even successful professionals to weigh the exit.
articles.image_caption: Travellers at an airport terminal; nearly 40% of Indian Americans say they have considered leaving the US
articles.nri_angle: For 5.2 million people of Indian origin in the US, a survey showing 40% have considered leaving puts hard data to a private unease about belonging — and signals a possible realignment of talent between the country that drew them and the India now courting them back.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: New York Moves to Make August 15 India Independence Day. For the Diaspora, It's a Marker of Arrival.
articles.excerpt: The State Senate has urged Governor Kathy Hochul to proclaim the date statewide, with lawmakers calling the Indian-American community 'woven into the fabric' of New York — a recognition that lands in a year of unease about belonging.
articles.image_caption: New York Governor Kathy Hochul, whom the State Senate has urged to proclaim August 15 as India Independence Day
articles.nri_angle: A state officially recognising August 15 folds a private diaspora observance into America's public civic calendar — a marker of arrival for the second-largest US immigrant group, and a counter-signal of belonging in a year when surveys show parts of the community feeling unsettled.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Doubled the Rate on NRI Dollar Deposits. Now the Diaspora Is Racing to Break Its Old Ones.
articles.excerpt: The RBI has lifted rate caps on fresh NRE and FCNR(B) deposits until September 30th, pushing dollar yields to 7%. Existing depositors are stuck at the old rates — and scrambling to rebook.
articles.image_caption: Nick Kenrick.. via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs hold dollar and rupee deposits in Indian banks; the RBI's temporary rate-cap removal turns a sleepy savings instrument into a time-limited 7% opportunity — but only for fresh money, forcing existing depositors to weigh premature-withdrawal penalties before the September 30th window shuts.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Telugu Conventions in One Summer: How a Language Spoken 8,000 Miles Away Refuses to Fade in America
articles.excerpt: Thousands of Telugu families gather near Philadelphia this weekend for the MATA convention — one of four rival national gatherings this summer, and a working census of one of America's most organised diaspora communities.
articles.image_caption: An Indian classical dancer in performance; Telugu-American conventions pair cultural showcases with business, immigration and youth forums.
articles.nri_angle: The Telugu-American community sustains four competing national conventions in a single summer — a feat of organisation driven by a generational anxiety over whether language, ritual and identity survive the handover to children raised entirely on American soil.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Has a New Job for Its 35 Million Emigrants: Sell the Country to Their Foreign Friends
articles.excerpt: From Modi's 'Chalo India' campaign to MakeMyTrip's 'India: The Homecoming,' New Delhi is recasting the diaspora as an unpaid, emotionally invested tourism sales force. The flattery comes with weight.
articles.image_caption: Nick Kenrick.. via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: A cluster of government and corporate campaigns is asking overseas Indians to convert homeland affection into tourism bookings and to act as trust brokers persuading non-Indian friends to visit — instrumentalising a relationship many emigrants experience as private and unresolved.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Made Its NRI Savings Accounts the Best Deal in Years. The Window Closes September 30.
articles.excerpt: The RBI scrapped interest-rate caps on NRE and FCNR(B) deposits, and banks are already offering 7%. The fine print is where the diaspora should look twice.
articles.image_caption: Nick Kenrick.. via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: For overseas Indians, parking money back home has always been about more than yield. A temporary RBI relaxation now pairs that sentiment with the most competitive deposit rates in years—and a short clock.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: France Is Getting Its First Traditional Hindu Temple, Carved in India and Rebuilt Stone by Stone Near Paris
articles.excerpt: A community builds in permanent stone when it has decided it is staying. In a country defined by laïcité, that is a particularly pointed statement.
articles.image_caption: A BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, built in the traditional carved-stone style France's new temple will share.
articles.nri_angle: A temple carved in India and reassembled in Europe is a literal rendering of what the diaspora does with its heritage—carrying the original across an ocean and rebuilding it as an anchor for the next generation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora Wants to Build India's Story a Permanent Home in Washington. It Will Cost $14 Million.
articles.excerpt: After eight years of quiet research, the team behind the India Heritage Center is launching an aggressive campaign for a 20,000-square-foot museum in the US capital — ten galleries tracing 11,000 years of civilisation, aimed as much at mainstream America as at the next generation of Indian-Americans.
articles.image_caption: A museum in Washington, DC; the proposed India Heritage Center would join the capital's cultural institutions
articles.nri_angle: A proposed $14 million India Heritage Center in Washington would give the Indian-American story its first permanent civilisational museum in the US — a test of whether a community that has succeeded materially will fund its own cultural memory for the next generation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Connecticut Diaspora Chapter Turned 20. Its Guest List Was a Map of How Far Indian-Americans Have Come.
articles.excerpt: GOPIO-CT honored a state senator, a bank CEO, and three others at its 20th anniversary gala — and gave away $50,000 to two non-Indian local charities in the process.
articles.image_caption: Hands raise a trophy skyward, evoking the awards presented at a community recognition gala
articles.nri_angle: For Indian-Americans, founding a cultural association is easy; keeping one alive for two decades is the hard part. GOPIO-CT's milestone shows what it takes for an immigrant community organization to outlive its founders and graduate from Diwali dinners to public policy, youth charity, and a recognized voice in state affairs.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's Oldest Indian Association Honored Seven 'Jewels.' The List Doubled as a Census of the Diaspora.
articles.excerpt: Founded in 1967, AIA-NY has watched the entire arc of Indian migration to America. Its 2026 gala honored oncologists, a transplant pioneer, and a Harvard MBA building an AI startup.
articles.image_caption: kevin dooley via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: An honoree list is a quiet census. AIA-NY's seven 'Ratnas' track exactly where Indian-Americans have concentrated — heavy in medicine, rising in tech and finance — while documenting a generational handoff from five-decade veterans to a 20-something founder. It also shows the value of an institution that has outlasted six decades of arrivals.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora's Most Remarkable 2025 Election Win Came From an Island of 1.4 Million — and a Great-Granddaughter of Indentured Laborers
articles.excerpt: Kamla Persad-Bissessar, sworn in for a second term as Trinidad and Tobago's prime minister, complicates the Silicon-Valley story of Indian success abroad with a far older one.
articles.image_caption: Kamla Persad-Bissessar, prime minister of Trinidad and Tobago and a descendant of Indian indentured laborers
articles.nri_angle: The dominant narrative of the Indian diaspora fixates on recent, professional, US-and-UK arrivals. Trinidad's 180-year-old Indian community — descendants of indentured estate laborers — is the diaspora's longest experiment in what Indian identity becomes after a century and a half away from India. Persad-Bissessar's return puts that story back at the center.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: She Was in Third Place on Election Night. A Week of Counting Made Her a Contender to Run Los Angeles.
articles.excerpt: Coimbatore-born councilmember Nithya Raman overtook a reality-TV upstart to reach the November runoff against Mayor Karen Bass — a race that could put a daughter of the diaspora atop America's second-largest city.
articles.image_caption: Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman, who advanced to the November mayoral runoff against incumbent Karen Bass
articles.nri_angle: More than a million South Asians live in California, the largest such population in the U.S. A Raman victory in November would place an Indian-born immigrant at the head of Los Angeles, its $15B budget and the 2028 Olympics — a marker of how far Indian-American political power has moved from the margins to the center.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ten Galleries, Eleven Thousand Years: The Diaspora's Plan to Build India a Museum in Washington
articles.excerpt: After eight years of planning, organizers are launching a campaign for the India Heritage Center — what would be the first U.S. institution devoted entirely to India's civilizational story.
articles.image_caption: A museum gallery interior, illustrating the kind of immersive exhibition space planned for the proposed India Heritage Center
articles.nri_angle: A permanent national museum answers a problem the diaspora keeps solving in pieces — how to pass a civilizational inheritance to a second generation fluent in American life but distant from its roots. It also tests whether a community that gives generously to universities and temples will fund a slower, less personal kind of cultural infrastructure.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Twenty Years On, a King Still Toasts the Diaspora That Helped Him Build a Charity
articles.excerpt: King Charles III joined the British Asian Trust's 20th-anniversary gala in London, where the diaspora-funded charity raised over £1 million and underscored how Britain's wealthiest minority became a donor class.
articles.image_caption: King Charles III, Royal Founding Patron of the British Asian Trust, which marked its 20th anniversary in London
articles.nri_angle: The British Asian Trust inverts the old migrant narrative: instead of remitting earnings home, Britain's 1.9 million Indian-origin residents now pool wealth through a British institution to fund South Asian development — a marker of a community confident enough in its standing to give at scale.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Town of 25,000 Is About to Host 8,000 Sikhs. Squamish's Nagar Kirtan Returns After the Fire.
articles.excerpt: A mountain resort town north of Vancouver revives its Sikh procession on June 20, two years after a wildfire cancelled it — and turns a 17th-century martyrdom into a fixture of the civic calendar.
articles.image_caption: A Nagar Kirtan procession winds through the streets, devotees following the float carrying the Guru Granth Sahib
articles.nri_angle: For Sikhs in British Columbia, carrying the faith out of the gurdwara and onto a small town's main street is how a visible minority converts private devotion into public belonging — and the langar does the explaining a sermon cannot.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four Million Jains, Eight Hundred Teenagers, One New Jersey Ballroom: How a Tiny Faith Refuses to Thin Out
articles.excerpt: The 17th Young Jains of America convention, July 2-5, is one of the largest gatherings of Jain youth outside India — and a case study in how a small diaspora fights the third-generation problem.
articles.image_caption: An ornately carved Jain temple, the kind of architectural tradition the diaspora works to keep meaningful for youth raised abroad
articles.nri_angle: Too small to rely on ambient culture or dense temple networks, Jains in North America have to organize their faith's survival deliberately — making the YJA convention a sharp, instructive version of the transmission problem every diaspora family faces.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: In the House of Lords, Sixty People Gathered to Argue That Diaspora Poetry Belongs in the Building
articles.excerpt: An evening hosted by Lord Bhikhu Parekh honoured English-language poets of the Indian diaspora — a body of work long caught between two literary worlds and claimed by neither.
articles.image_caption: Lord Bhikhu Parekh, the political theorist and crossbench peer who hosted the diaspora poetry evening at the House of Lords
articles.nri_angle: British Indians are now the UK's wealthiest minority and an established political force, but their writers have yet to win a settled place in the nation's cultural memory — and this gathering was a bid to close that gap, one publishing contract at a time.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Why NRI Money Is Pouring Back Into Indian Property
articles.excerpt: A softer rupee, a premium-housing boom and a $1.6bn institutional surge are pulling diaspora capital toward Indian real estate in 2026.
articles.image_caption: Mumbai's skyline; premium residential supply in India's metros is drawing returning and investing NRIs (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Explains the 2026 surge in NRI real-estate investment in India, the currency and supply dynamics driving it, the Gulf diaspora's role, and the risks diaspora buyers face purchasing from abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A New Jersey Temple Raises Funds, and Makes a Case for Belonging
articles.excerpt: At the Shree Siddhivinayak Temple in Toms River, a community-hall campaign reflects the diaspora's shift from building places of worship to building institutions.
articles.image_caption: Diaspora temples increasingly serve as cultural and community centres, not only places of worship.
articles.nri_angle: Chronicles how an immigrant-founded temple in New Jersey is building institutions to retain second-generation Indian-Americans, a pattern across the North American diaspora, with Indian consular backing.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: In Paris, Modi Closes a European Tour Among the Diaspora
articles.excerpt: A community address and a VivaTech pavilion turn the final leg of an India-France visit into a courtship of expatriate talent and capital.
articles.image_caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who addressed the Indian community in Paris on June 18 during the final leg of his European tour.
articles.nri_angle: Directly addresses France's ~119,000-strong Indian community and the broader use of diaspora outreach as an instrument of Indian statecraft, including remittance flows and tech-talent recruitment via VivaTech.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian-Born Banker Will Run America's Fifth-Largest Bank. The Diaspora Has Run Out of First Times to Celebrate.
articles.excerpt: Gunjan Kedia takes the helm at U.S. Bancorp this spring, becoming the first Indian American to lead a top-tier U.S. bank. The milestone is striking precisely because the diaspora is running out of ceilings to break.
articles.image_caption: The U.S. Bancorp Center in Minneapolis, headquarters of the bank Gunjan Kedia will lead as CEO.
articles.nri_angle: Indian Americans have long dominated the C-suites of American technology and consumer goods. Banking, the most conservative corner of corporate America, was the last big holdout — and a diaspora woman just took its keys.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nine Million Indians Abroad Sent Home $138 Billion. A Proposed 5% U.S. Tax Could Take a Bite Out of It.
articles.excerpt: India remains the world's largest remittance recipient by a wide margin. But a proposed American levy on outbound transfers, and a volatile balance of payments, are reminding everyone how exposed those diaspora dollars really are.
articles.image_caption: Indian rupee notes and coins — remittances now exceed $135 billion a year, the largest such flow in the world.
articles.nri_angle: For the NRI sending money to parents in Kerala or a sister's wedding in Lucknow, remittances are personal. In aggregate they are macroeconomic infrastructure — and policy in Washington and Delhi now treats the diaspora's money as a strategic asset to be courted or taxed.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A TV Host Mocked Indians for Loving Mangoes. The Diaspora's Reply Was a Lesson in What 'Home' Tastes Like.
articles.excerpt: A throwaway segment ridiculing the WhatsApp groups Indian Americans use to buy seasonal mangoes turned into a referendum on belonging — and on how a single fruit carries an entire community's idea of home.
articles.image_caption: A heap of ripe yellow mangoes on display — the seasonal fruit at the centre of a diaspora identity row.
articles.nri_angle: Few things capture the diaspora's split existence like the summer mango hunt — the WhatsApp coordination, the costly imported boxes, the ritual of tasting a flavour from childhood thousands of miles from where it grew. When that ritual was mocked, the reaction revealed how much identity a community can pack into a fruit.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Four of the University of Florida's Top Professors This Year Took the Same Road From India. That's Not a Coincidence.
articles.excerpt: Kshitij Khare, Desika Narayanan, Jasmeet Judge, and Paramita Chakrabarty span statistics, astrophysics, remote sensing, and Alzheimer's research — and a tenth of one university's highest research honors going to Indian-origin scholars reveals the quiet infrastructure of diaspora influence.
articles.image_caption: The University of Florida in Gainesville, where four India-born scholars made the 2026 list of honored professors
articles.nri_angle: The four UFRF professors expose the diaspora's least-visible layer of influence — not the headline CEO or senator, but the tenured researchers who train PhDs, win federal grants, and run the labs that keep American universities at the frontier, built on intellectual capital that Indian institutions trained and exported.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Google Just Picked Its First Class of Junior Faculty Stars. One of Them Is Teaching Computers to Design Computer Chips.
articles.excerpt: Arizona State's Vidya Chhabria won an inaugural Google ML and Systems award and $100,000 in unrestricted funding — a spotlight on the diaspora's deepest and least-visible groove in American technology: the engineers who design the chips everyone else runs on.
articles.image_caption: Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (CC)
articles.nri_angle: Chhabria's award redirects attention from the diaspora's celebrated tech executives to its foundational engineering layer — the Indian-origin researchers who have long populated electronic design automation and semiconductor labs, a lineage that now sits at the center of the world's most strategically contested technology.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Britain's Wealthiest Minority Just Told Its Politicians: We Are Done Being Taken for Granted
articles.excerpt: The British Indian Census 2025, presented at Parliament this month, finds a 1.8-million-strong community whose political loyalty is now genuinely up for grabs — and whose patience with being a 'tick-box exercise' has run out.
articles.image_caption: The Houses of Parliament and Big Ben in London
articles.nri_angle: For a community that measured success in incomes and degrees, the 2025 census marks a shift from being a statistic others quote to a constituency others must answer to — with loyalty leaking toward smaller parties and an unresolved question of belonging surfacing even at Parliament.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Man Tore an Indian Flag Outside a Texas City Hall. Six Members of Congress Decided It Was a Safety Story.
articles.excerpt: In Frisco, where one in three residents is now Asian, a viral act of contempt has forced the Indian American community to confront a question its success was supposed to settle: does it belong?
articles.image_caption: The Indian national tricolour (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The flag-tearing has shifted how Indian Americans talk about belonging — from offense to fear — and shows a maturing diaspora willing to push back publicly through its largest-ever congressional delegation rather than keep its head down.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Passed England as Australia's Largest Migrant Group. The Margin Was a Few Dozen People; the Trend Is Generational.
articles.excerpt: With 971,020 India-born residents and a median age two decades younger than the English-born population, the diaspora is no longer assimilating into Australia's story — it is helping write the next one.
articles.image_caption: Sydney, Australia; Indians have become the country's largest migrant group (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Becoming Australia's single largest migrant group means the Indian community is now a founding partner in what the country becomes — its weekend language schools, temples, and cricket leagues are the infrastructure of a population that expects to stay for generations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 'Grateful for Your Concern About the Diaspora': Modi and Carney Just Turned a Two-Year Freeze Into a Trade Ambition
articles.excerpt: Their fourth meeting in under a year targets a doubling of India-Canada trade by 2030 — but for 1.8 million Indo-Canadians, the real prize is the restoration of the visas and family ties a diplomatic collapse had frozen.
articles.image_caption: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, official portrait
articles.nri_angle: The India-Canada thaw is, in practice, a diaspora deal: the trade talks center on talent mobility, education, and people-to-people ties, and a working diplomatic relationship means 1.8 million Indo-Canadians are no longer hostage to a single accusation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
